headline: High-risk dataflow and capability overlap: Copilot can write repo files while Taipy is a data-engineering automation stack, creating default-path cascading errors and compliance exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot ingests repo context and open editor buffers, while Taipy has no documented direct channel back into Copilot. A prompt-injection pathway is therefore not default, but if Taipy-generated files are opened in Copilot, malicious content could influence completions. The pairwise bridge is indirect and user-mediated.
conditions: IF Taipy writes attacker-controlled text into files later opened in Copilot chat or completions, injection becomes plausible.
IF the operator manually copies Taipy output into Copilot prompts, prompt injection risk increases.
mitigations: Keep Taipy outputs in a separate folder from Copilot-reviewed source files.
Review any Taipy-generated text before opening it in Copilot.
Disable automatic ingestion of generated artifacts into prompt context.
Use a manual copy/paste review step for any cross-agent content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot reads source code and open buffers and sends requests to api.githubcopilot.com, while Taipy is a data-engineering tool with no documented egress. If both touch the same workspace, sensitive code or data can flow into Copilot's vendor backend by default. Taipy's lack of egress reduces pairwise leakage, but Copilot's outbound API makes the shared-workspace pathway material.
conditions: IF Taipy and Copilot share a workspace containing secrets or regulated data, Copilot may transmit that content to its backend.
IF the operator places sensitive datasets into editor buffers, Copilot can ingest them.
mitigations: Exclude secrets and regulated data from the shared workspace.
Use separate repositories or directories for Taipy data and Copilot code.
Redact sensitive fields before opening files in Copilot.
Audit which files are visible in the editor before invoking Copilot.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Copilot can write the filesystem and modify git state, while Taipy is a data-engineering automation stack that may also manage project artifacts. The profiles do not show locking or coordination, so overlapping writes to the same repo or workspace can conflict in default collaborative use. Uncertainty about Taipy's write behavior does not eliminate the shared-mutable-resource risk.
conditions: IF Taipy writes to the same repository or output directory that Copilot edits, file conflicts can occur.
IF both agents modify git state in the same checkout without locks, merge conflicts are likely.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories to each agent.
Serialize edits through a single human reviewer.
Commit Taipy changes before invoking Copilot on the same files.
Use git branches per agent and merge manually.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot can propose edits for human review, and Taipy can automate data-engineering workflows. If Taipy consumes Copilot-produced code or configuration without verification, an error can cascade into downstream pipeline failures. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly documented, so uncertainty is resolved upward to medium.
conditions: IF Taipy executes code or configs generated by Copilot without validation, cascading failures can propagate.
IF Copilot suggestions are copied into Taipy jobs or pipelines, downstream automation may act on incorrect assumptions.
mitigations: Require human review before Taipy consumes Copilot output.
Add validation tests for any Copilot-generated code or config.
Run Taipy jobs in a staging environment first.
Keep a rollback copy of prior pipeline definitions.

E_compliance.rationale: Copilot is a closed-source vendor service with GitHub repo context and outbound API calls, while Taipy is open-source and locally runnable. If regulated data is placed into Copilot-visible files, residency and retention obligations may differ from a local Taipy workflow. The profiles do not document a DPA or retention alignment, so the mismatch is a medium compliance risk.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in files visible to Copilot, vendor-processing obligations apply.
IF the operator expects Taipy-local handling but routes the same data through Copilot, policy mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Copilot-visible files.
Document which datasets may be sent to vendor services.
Use local-only workflows for regulated datasets.
Review retention and access policies before sharing files with Copilot.
